quote: Looks like you filled out some information on the 20.
stewart_read: The rep's legitimacy answer is vague ('the 20' with no month, no source website named) instead of the honest_specificity pattern the schema calls for. On a call that opens with immediate suspicion, this is the moment that should have anchored trust and doesn't.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to always have a specific, repeatable legitimacy line ready — source website name, approximate date with month, and campaign context — rather than a generic 'you filled out a form' claim that invites further doubt.

quote: I've you just gave me, like, basic info, like address, contact info.
stewart_read: This is the second touch of the same unresolved legitimacy dispute — the rep repeats the unverified claim in different words rather than offering new, specific evidence, so the customer's suspicion is never actually addressed.
coaching_implication: Show the rep this exact exchange as an example of restating instead of resolving — the fix is a concrete detail (date, source), not a rephrase of the same vague claim.

stewart_read: This is a textbook trigger for the 'I can't afford it' flip ('what you can't afford is your current bill'), but the rep instead leads with the no-upfront-cost feature claim, which the customer immediately rejects again at 01:21.
alternative_hypothesis: A reactive read would say the rep simply didn't have time to flip before the customer cut in again — but the rep had a full turn to respond and chose the feature-pitch path, so this is a missed technique, not a timing issue.
coaching_implication: Drill the objection_inversion flip specifically for 'I don't have money' / 'can't afford it' language — this customer said it twice and the rep never attempted the reframe.

quote: How much every month have to pay?
stewart_read: The customer is directly asking for a number — a real curiosity signal — and the rep's answer ('there isn't necessarily a rough idea or ballpark') closes the door on curiosity rather than using the ambiguity to create it (e.g., tying the eventual design reveal to their specific bill).
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: schema's price_estimate_before_design rebuttal explicitly avoids giving a ballpark, so declining a number is procedurally correct.
coaching_implication: The rep followed the no-ballpark rule correctly, but delivered it flatly ('it's very different home to home') instead of redirecting to curiosity about their own bill/usage — coach the redirect language, not the refusal itself.

quote: But I don't have I I'm I'm I'm renting. Who who told you that I have a house?
stewart_read: The renter disclosure is a hard DQ, but it arrives only because the customer volunteered it under challenge — the rep never proactively ran the homeowner-confirmation verify step earlier in the call, which would have surfaced this in the first 30 seconds instead of at 02:35.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: the rep may have assumed homeownership from the lead form data and saw no reason to re-ask — but the customer had already denied filling out the form at 00:38, which should have prompted a homeowner re-check well before 02:35.
coaching_implication: Once a customer disputes the form's origin, the rep should immediately re-verify basic qualifiers (homeowner status) rather than continuing into program pitch — this would have DQ'd the call two minutes earlier and saved floor time.

quote: Well, it's on the form that was filled out. That's the only reason I'm calling is because someone put the information on, but I'll just go ahead and remove you.
stewart_read: The call ends with an apology-and-removal exit and no attempt to identify who actually submitted the lead (a family member, a data-entry error, etc.) — a missed chance to correct the record or salvage the lead source data.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read is the stronger fit here — there is no strategic reason to skip a quick clarifying question ('do you know who else might live there and could have filled this out?') before closing; the rep simply exited fast.
coaching_implication: On disputed-lead-source DQs, coach a single clarifying question before removal — it costs 10 seconds and either corrects bad data or confirms the DQ cleanly.
